title: Foundations: Jazz Ballads - The Complete Guide
summary: What Jazz Ballads is, where it came from, and how its songs work.
body:
Jazz Ballads songs: Jazz ballads are slow, exposed, and honest: a singer and a few instruments telling a love story at 60 beats per minute. Every breath matters; every note is a choice.

History: Billie Holiday's late-1950s recordings, Johnny Hartman's with Coltrane (1963), and Chet Baker's fragile vocals defined the art. Singers still prove themselves on ballads.

How the songs work: Jazz Ballads favors the keys of Eb, F, Bb, C. Common forms include Single chorus, rubato intro; Verse–chorus with an instrumental bridge. Players should master rubato: stretching time at the song's edges first, then back-phrasing: landing the lyric after the beat. Piano and archtop guitar territory.

title: My Funny Valentine - Jazz Ballads Song Study
summary: Harmonic blueprint and playing guide for My Funny Valentine by Richard Rodgers (1937).
body:
My Funny Valentine — Richard Rodgers, 1937. Chet Baker's fragile 1954 version is definitive.

HARMONIC BLUEPRINT (study chart, key of Bb):
A#m7b5 | D#7 | G#m | G#m

This study chart uses the 'Minor ballad' progression, the Jazz Ballads workhorse, to map how songs like this move. Form: single chorus, rubato intro. Listen for minimal vibrato until the emotional peak — it is the fingerprint of the style.

TO PLAY IT: set your tempo to the Jazz Ballads pocket, voice the chords cleanly, and let minimal vibrato until the emotional peak. Piano and archtop guitar territory. (Song facts: title/artist/year are documented public records; the chart is an original study arrangement.)
